object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A reported event where some aspect of the system is not working correctly. Created when something breaks and is discovered via alert, customer report, or manual detection. Tracked through lifecycle states from triage through resolution.

source_references.excerpt: Something breaks. We find out about it, one way or another. Somebody declares an incident, somebody runs it, we fix it, we write it up.
Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence number.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical classification of impact scope, ranging from SEV1 (complete service outage affecting all users) to SEV4 (degraded functionality affecting limited scope).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Business urgency classification based on customer impact, customer expectations, and SLA obligations. Independent from severity (technical impact).

source_references.excerpt: priority is P1 through P4. Which is completely different, and this is the single biggest source of miscommunication in the company. Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The lifecycle state of an incident: triage (initial assessment), declared (confirmed and assigned), mitigated (fix applied), resolved (fix validated), closed (incident completed).

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander, that's the point of triage: someone's looking at whether this is even real. A commander is assigned when it's declared. If it turns out to be nothing, it gets closed from triage having never had one. That's the accurate version. Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A monitoring system notification that indicates a potential issue. Can be automatically generated by the monitoring platform or manually raised by an engineer. Every incident must be linked to at least one alert or customer ticket.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.
Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an alert, assigned by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A support system record created when a customer reports an issue. Every incident must be linked to at least one alert or customer ticket.

source_references.excerpt: a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.
I've tried, when someone's told me something in a corridor. You have to raise a ticket first and link it.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a support ticket, from the support system.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A backend system or component owned by a team. An incident affects one or more services. Identified by a unique name enforced in the service catalogue.

source_references.excerpt: The service owner is the team that owns the broken thing.
Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: The unique name identifier for a service.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: An organizational unit that owns one or more services. Teams are standing assignments responsible for systems.

inferred_constraints.description: An Incident cannot be a duplicate of itself.

source_references.excerpt: That's a strange question. No, obviously not. Someone did do it by accident. There was a bulk-linking script during the November mess and it linked one incident to itself and the dashboard divided by zero. Then it's worth stating. An incident cannot be a duplicate of itself.

inferred_constraints.description: The duplicate relationship should be acyclic: if Incident A is a duplicate of Incident B, then Incident B cannot (directly or indirectly) be a duplicate of Incident A. Duplicates should point directly to a primary, not form chains.

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. It's wrong. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A. When we roll up incident counts we only follow one hop, so a chain undercounts. So duplicates should point directly at a primary, and a primary is not itself a duplicate of anything. That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Incident commander optionality by state: The constraint on Incident is commanded by Person must be contextual to the IncidentState. Declared incidents have exactly one commander; triage incidents have zero. The model captures single-valued uniqueness on Incident but does not express the state-dependent mandatory participation. Should this be modeled as a conditional constraint (if state=declared then commander is mandatory), or as a separate fact type per state?

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority changes over time: The transcript indicates that both Severity and Priority can change during an incident's lifecycle (e.g., severity revised as blast radius becomes clear). The model captures the current values only. Whether the change history should be tracked via a timeline/event log, or whether only the current state is stored, requires clarification.

source_references.excerpt: Can either change during the incident? Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected. In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Incident cause classification and user-error incidents: There is ongoing disagreement about whether incidents later determined to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is. This decision has not been made and will be raised with Ravi. The model currently does not include any concept of cause classification because none has been formally adopted. Once a decision is made, a Cause or IncidentCause concept may need to be added.

source_references.excerpt: Support raises tickets. Some of those tickets become incidents. A meaningful number of those turn out to be user error -- the customer had misconfigured something, or they were on an old client, or they were doing something we never supported. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Alert and Ticket origin relationship direction: An Incident originates from an Alert or Ticket. The transcript does not clarify whether an Alert or Ticket can originate multiple Incidents (e.g., a customer ticket generates multiple distinct incidents), or whether the relationship is many-to-one or many-to-many. The model assumes many-to-many (an incident can originate from multiple alerts and/or tickets; an alert or ticket can originate multiple incidents) but this should be confirmed.

source_references.excerpt: Or both, which is the common one -- the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.
